title: The Unshared Horizon
relation: Ancient brothers divided over foresight, refusal, and concealed possibility
summary: Aethon and Kairoth once compared the farthest light with the hour at which a traveler should turn home. The First Concord required both kinds of attention. Its Sundering left their old conversation unfinished: a warning, an unshared possibility, and an argument about who is entitled to judge a cost. Their stories ask different questions of the same silence, without requiring a mortal to become the courier of either brother's grievance.

aa: Discovery and Patience bring the brothers to an inquiry neither can finish alone. Aethon asks to know the price of the withheld prevention before arguing about whether it should have been revealed. Kairoth names innocent lives erased, then acknowledges that his fear of the council's answer was a prediction about others, not their actual consent. Aethon does not mistake this admission for proof that the council would have found a harmless solution.

Your two choices establish a distinction between investigation and implementation. An account can be examined without turning its terrible option into a plan. Kairoth still fears that making a possibility intelligible makes it tempting; Aethon still fears that secrecy lets a single guardian define every acceptable future. They agree neither fear can have the last word merely because it is sincere. Elaris's questions about the chronology remain unanswered where evidence is absent. No recovered minute appears to reconcile the record. What changes is their willingness to mark that absence openly: not an invitation to erase anyone, and not a reason to stop asking. Their old chart has room for a boundary that can be discussed rather than worshiped.
ab: Discovery and Decisiveness make this a conversation about the warning that should accompany an option. Aethon wants every preventable danger named while action is still possible. Kairoth answers that an alternative described merely as prevention would have concealed its victims more effectively than silence. Innocent people erased from history cannot wait for a later correction to the announcement. Their lives belonged in its first sentence.

Aethon accepts the correction, but not the conclusion that only Kairoth was fit to hear the full sentence. Kairoth accepts that withholding it was his own intervention, not an absence of action. The brothers do not manufacture a demonstration of the rejected future or offer you access to it. They instead describe how they would speak about a dangerous possibility now: state the evidence, state the threatened lives, distinguish a decision from a prophecy. Such speech might still end in disagreement. Your choices have not guaranteed wise councils or timely trust. They have removed one excuse for silence and one excuse for haste. Aethon will not announce a solution stripped of its cost; Kairoth will not call another person's possible disagreement proof that conversation has already failed.
ba: Contemplation and Patience seem, at first, to offer the brothers a comfortable escape. They could sit together beneath an immense sky and let age make their quarrel sound small. Aethon is the one who interrupts that temptation. The catastrophe was not small to those who endured it, and the lives in Kairoth's rejected prevention were not small because no one here can give a complete account of them.

Kairoth acknowledges that waiting became a way to preserve control of his testimony. Aethon acknowledges that listening became impossible whenever his brother failed to say what he hoped to hear. Neither confession completes the missing chronology that Elaris disputes. The brothers agree to distinguish a pause needed for honest thought from a silence maintained to exhaust the questioner. It is a fragile agreement between beings practiced at making endurance sound virtuous. Your completed paths give it a mortal measure: both listening and waiting must leave the other person free to return with the question. They part without announcing that time has healed them. Time has provided no such verdict. For this conversation, they have merely stopped using its vastness to make an unfinished obligation disappear.
bb: Contemplation and Decisiveness place the brothers on different sides of a necessary pause. Aethon insists that a true warning may still need interpretation. Kairoth insists that an urgent refusal cannot always wait for complete agreement. Their old quarrel returns until they notice that neither statement authorizes concealing what has actually been chosen. Deliberation and action are not rival claims to own the account afterward.

Kairoth states his refusal of the erasing prevention without presenting it as the only imaginable moral intelligence. Aethon hears it without inventing a painless alternative to keep his accusation intact. He then asks about the withheld chronology, and Kairoth does not call the question a demand to sacrifice the innocents. Elaris's dispute remains a dispute; it supplies neither brother with a missing proof. Your paths have not brought the heavens and the clock into perfect agreement. They have given their conversation a sequence: listen to the warning, name the cost, state the choice, remain available for scrutiny. The last step is the one both neglected. It is also the only step still fully possible here, without asking any mortal life to be unwritten so that ancient brothers can feel reconciled.
